summary: Psalm 73 opens Book III with a crisis over the prosperity of the wicked. The speaker nearly slips into envy, describes arrogant people who seem secure, then reaches a turning point in God’s sanctuary and reconsiders their end. The poem closes with confession, renewed nearness to God, and a decision to make the Lord Yahweh his refuge.
whyItMatters: This chapter gives the collection a sharp wisdom problem at the start of Book III: if God is good, why do arrogant and violent people seem to flourish? It does not solve the question by denying the pain; it moves through envy, sanctuary reflection, and renewed trust.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by Asaph.” In Psalms, such headings can indicate authorship, association, collection, dedication, or belonging, and their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and instruction.
context.date: Psalm 73 cannot be securely assigned to a single date. It belongs to a Psalter whose poems and collections developed over centuries, from the monarchy through the postexilic period.
context.setting: Psalm 73 begins Book III, a section concerned with sanctuary, collapse, and hard questions about God’s rule. Within the poem, the speaker’s crisis turns when he enters God’s sanctuary.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using parallel lines, vivid images, shifts in address, confession, and wisdom reflection.

outline.heading: Opening claim and personal danger
outline.note: The psalm begins by affirming God’s goodness, then admits that envy of the arrogant nearly caused the speaker to slip.

outline.heading: The wicked appear secure
outline.note: The speaker describes the wicked as healthy, proud, violent, boastful, dismissive of God’s knowledge, and increasing in riches.

outline.heading: The speaker’s painful question
outline.note: He wonders whether purity and innocence have been vain, while also fearing that speaking this way would betray God’s children.

outline.heading: Sanctuary insight and the wicked’s end
outline.note: Entering God’s sanctuary changes the frame: the speaker considers the unstable and destructive end of those he had envied.

outline.heading: Confession and being held
outline.note: He admits grief, bitterness, and ignorance, yet says God has held him and will guide him.

outline.heading: God as portion and refuge
outline.note: The psalm ends by naming God as the speaker’s desire, strength, portion, refuge, and the one whose works he will tell.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm’s stated conviction before the speaker describes the crisis that nearly overturned it.

keyVerses.text: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
keyVerses.why: This names the emotional and moral problem that drives the chapter: the speaker sees wicked people prospering and envies them.

keyVerses.text: until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end.
keyVerses.why: This is the turning point of the poem, where the speaker’s perspective changes.

keyVerses.text: My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the closing confession: the speaker’s security is no longer the visible prosperity he had envied, but God himself.

questions.question: Who is Asaph?
questions.answer: The heading says, “A Psalm by Asaph.” In 1 Chronicles, Asaph is a Levite appointed to lead praise before the ark, and his sons continue in musical service. The heading connects this psalm with that worship tradition, while the broader range of psalm headings leaves open whether the name marks personal authorship or a collection associated with him.

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with confidence if the speaker is about to struggle?
questions.answer: Verse 1 states the conviction that God is good to Israel and to the pure in heart. Verses 2-3 then reveal that the speaker’s own experience felt unstable because he envied the prosperity of the wicked. The poem lets the settled claim and the honest crisis stand beside each other.

questions.question: What does “my feet were almost gone” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase is an image for nearly losing moral or spiritual footing. The next line, “My steps had nearly slipped,” makes the image clearer. The danger is not a literal fall but the speaker’s near collapse into envy and confusion.

questions.question: What makes the wicked look so tempting to the speaker?
questions.answer: The speaker says they seem free from ordinary burdens, firm in strength, always at ease, and increasing in riches. He also portrays them as proud, violent, malicious, and arrogant. The scandal is that their wrongdoing does not appear, at first, to prevent their comfort or influence.

questions.question: Are the wicked denying that God knows what happens?
questions.answer: Verse 11 reports their words: “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” The psalm depicts them speaking as if God’s knowledge or attention can be questioned. It presents this as part of their arrogance, not as the speaker’s final view.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say purity may have been “in vain”?
questions.answer: In verses 13-14 he compares his own attempts at innocence with his daily trouble. From his limited view, the wicked prosper while he is “plagued” and “punished every morning.” The chapter treats this as a painful perception the speaker is wrestling through, not as the poem’s final conclusion.

questions.question: What changes in God’s sanctuary?
questions.answer: Verse 17 says the speaker entered God’s sanctuary and considered the wicked’s “latter end.” The text does not describe every detail of what he saw or heard there, but it marks a change from present appearances to ultimate outcome. After that, the prosperity he envied looks unstable and temporary.

questions.question: Why does the speaker call himself a “brute beast”?
questions.answer: After the turning point, he looks back on his bitterness and ignorance with shame. “Brute beast” is his own severe image for how senseless he had been before God. The next verse keeps the confession from despair: even then, he says, God held his right hand.

questions.question: Does the ending erase the earlier suffering?
questions.answer: No. Verse 26 still says, “My flesh and my heart fails,” so the speaker does not pretend weakness has disappeared. What changes is where he locates strength and security: God becomes his strength, portion, refuge, and the one whose works he will tell.

glossary.def: A Levite associated with musical praise in 1 Chronicles. His name heads this psalm and a group of poems connected with his worship tradition.
The people named in verse 1 as recipients of God’s goodness. In this chapter, the phrase is later echoed by the speaker’s concern about cleansing his heart.
The group the speaker envies and then reevaluates. They are described as prosperous, proud, violent, boastful, and far from God.
The place the speaker enters in verse 17. It marks the turning point where he begins to consider the end of those he had envied.
The word the speaker uses for God in verse 26. It presents God as his lasting share or inheritance when his own flesh and heart fail.
